The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
The Democratic victories in the mid-term elections
have Republicans re-examining their strategy going forward.
Kevin Roberts, with the Conservative Heritage Foundation,
says the Iran war clearly had an impact
on the outcome of the election.
The Trump administration inherited very high inflation
from the previous administration,
and all of those economic measures
were improving the week before the war in Iran.
In fact, our chief economist at Heritage, Dr. E.J. Antony,
has predicted that there would have been
a Trump economic boom had he not started the war in Iran.
The point is that Iran,
especially by increasing energy prices,
aggravated those inflationary pressures.
Roberts, who was a key architect
of the conservative blueprint Project 2025,
also praised President Trump's decision
to elevate advisor Stephen Miller
to be the new White House chief of staff.
He will replace Suzy Wiles.
The first major winter storm has struck Gaza,
bringing with it a crisis that humanitarian aid groups
have long been fearing.
The storm follows years of restrictions
on aid and reconstruction,
so that even a single night of heavy rain
has overwhelmed the displacement sites.
NPR's Anas Baba has the story.
- Throughout the night, displaced families across Gaza
were moving their belongings,
trying to keep floodwaters from entering their tents.
Floodwaters swept through main streets across Gaza,
while hundreds of displaced tents
were flooded or blown away.
Gaza Civil Defense says
it's received 2,200 emergency call overnights,
responding to collapsing structures
and families trapped in flood tents.
Israel says Gaza pre-winter humanitarian situation
is the best since the war began.
However, humanitarian agencies have warned that Israeli
restrictions on essential supplies like tents
and winterization materials
have left 1.3 million displaced people
at high risk of flooding.
Anas Baba, NPR News, Gaza City.
- It was a rocky week on Wall Street.
Investors weighed the results of the midterms,
a better-than-expected jobs report,
and fresh concerns about the boom
of artificial intelligence.
NPR's Scott Horsley has details.
- Stocks initially rallied after the election.
Once it became clear, Democrats had won decisively,
putting to rest fears of a disputed outcome
or a period of limbo.
But after buying stocks on Wednesday,
investors turned around and dumped them the following day.
Political setbacks for data centers
added to existing worries about the massive investment
in artificial intelligence,
the sell-off that began with tech stocks
quickly spread to the wider market.
There was a partial rebound on Friday
after the Labor Department reported solid job gains
for October, but all the major stock indexes
ended down for the week.
The Dow fell nearly 1%.
The S&P 500 index dropped 2 2/3%,
and the NASDAQ tumbled more than 3%.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
- You're listening to NPR.
- Voters have passed a Colorado ballot measure
replacing a flat state income tax rate
with a graduated income tax.
Colorado Public Radio's John Daly has the details.
- Amendment 87 will increase taxes
on Colorado's wealthiest residents and businesses,
those making more than half a million dollars a year,
raising more than $2 billion annually
for a state budget in crisis.
It will also lower the tax rate
for the least wealthy Coloradans.
Kathy White, with the group Protect Colorado's Future,
thanked voters who studied tax tables and said--
- This is good for me, it's good for my neighbors,
and I'm voting yes.
(cheering)
- The Colorado Chamber says the change
will make the state less competitive
and force businesses to make tough decisions.
Most of these changes will take effect next spring
in preparation for the 2027 tax year.
For NPR News, I'm John Daly in Denver.
- NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class
that will help grow the Artemis program,
focusing on lunar exploration.
Presently, the program has only 32 active astronauts,
but it needs more recruits to continue the mission.
Aspiring astronauts have between now and December 3rd
to submit their applications.
NASA expects to make its final selection by late 2027,
with the new candidates beginning their training
by early 2028.
NASA's last call for new astronauts was two years ago,
and at that time, more than 8,000 people applied,
but only 10 people made the final cut.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.
